title: Artifacts
description: The physiologic and non-physiologic artifacts of childhood, the rhythmic artifacts of the NICU and PICU, and a method for proving that a waveform is not cerebral.
why: Children move, feed and cry through their recordings, and rhythmic artifact in the NICU and PICU can look like a seizure.
objectives: Recognize the artifacts experts rated most important for residents to know, led by ECG, eye blinks, electrode pop and muscle.
Recognize the rhythmic artifacts of infancy and critical care, and confirm them on video.
Use field and physiology to decide whether a waveform is cerebral.

sections.title: Why artifact comes before abnormality
sections.content:
Every abnormality you will learn in the later modules has an artifact that imitates it. A sharp transient can be an electrode pop. Rhythmic activity can be a ventilator. Slow waves can be sweat. Before a waveform is called cerebral, the reader has to have excluded the non-cerebral explanations, and in a child that exclusion is harder than in a still adult, because children blink, chew, cry, suck, and are patted, rocked and fed through their recordings.

When experts were asked which EEG findings residents must know, the artifacts they rated most important were **ECG, eye blinks, electrode pop and muscle** ([Nascimento 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35904042/)). Those four are the commonest, the most often over-read, and the easiest to prove once you know what to look for. This module adds the artifacts specific to infancy and to the intensive care unit, where rhythmic artifact is the main imitator of seizures.

**The single most useful rule**

A cerebral discharge has a **plausible field**: a maximum at one electrode with smaller deflections at its neighbours, falling off with distance in a way that makes anatomical sense. An artifact usually does not. This is the sixth of the IFCN criteria for an epileptiform discharge, the scalp distribution that implies a source in the brain, and [[m05-variants|Module 5]] applies it to the question of over-reading. It is worth learning here first, because it resolves most artifact questions on its own. A waveform confined to a single electrode, or one that appears in electrodes that are not neighbours, or one whose distribution matches a piece of equipment rather than a piece of cortex, is not cerebral until proven otherwise.

The second rule is **physiology**: an artifact is generated by something, and that something can usually be found. The heart leaves a trace on the ECG channel. The eyes can be seen on video. A ventilator has a set rate. Finding the generator is the proof, and the artifact table in this module lists where to look for each one.
keyPoints: Experts rated ECG, eye blinks, electrode pop and muscle as the artifacts residents most need to know (Nascimento 2022).
A cerebral discharge has a plausible field that spreads to neighbouring electrodes; an artifact usually does not (IFCN criterion 6).
An artifact has a generator that can usually be found: the ECG channel, the video, the ventilator setting.
Exclude the non-cerebral explanations before calling any waveform abnormal.

question.question: A resident reviewing a routine EEG in a 5-year-old finds a sharply contoured transient and wants to call it a spike. Which single question, answered first, most efficiently decides whether it could be cerebral?
options: Is the transient present in more than one page of the record?
Does the transient have an after-going slow wave?
Does the transient have a plausible field, with a maximum at one electrode and smaller deflections at its neighbours?
Does the transient occur during hyperventilation?
question.explanation: The field is the first and most efficient test, because a waveform without a plausible scalp distribution cannot have a cerebral source regardless of its shape or timing, and most artifacts fail it. Recurrence across pages does not separate artifact from discharge; electrode pops and ECG artifact recur throughout a record. An after-going slow wave is one of the IFCN criteria but it is a morphology question that only matters once the field is plausible. Timing with hyperventilation says something about activation of a discharge, not about whether the transient is cerebral in the first place.

sections.title: Physiologic artifacts: eyes, muscle, heart and skin
sections.content:
Most artifact in a child comes from the child. Each physiologic artifact has a recognizable appearance and a way to confirm it.

**Eye blink.** The cornea is positive relative to the retina, and the eye rotates upward with a blink, so the positive pole moves toward the frontal electrodes. In a bipolar montage this produces a **symmetric downward deflection at Fp1 and Fp2**. The field is frontal only, with nothing posterior, and the eyes can be watched on video.

**Lateral eye movement.** A horizontal saccade moves the positive cornea toward one side, producing **opposite polarity at F7 and F8**, a mirror image across the hemispheres. **Brief lateral rectus spikes** at the start of each saccade can imitate frontotemporal sharp waves; their mirror-image distribution gives them away.

**Muscle.** Frontalis and temporalis contraction produces **very fast, spiky activity**, often temporal, during chewing, crying or grimacing. It disappears in sleep or with relaxation. Filtered muscle is the classic imitator of spikes, as [[m01-signals|Module 1]] warned: lowering the high-frequency filter rounds it into sharply contoured waves.

**ECG.** The heart's electrical field reaches the scalp, producing a **sharp transient time-locked to the QRS**, often prominent in infants because the heart is close and the head is small. It is proved by lining the transient up with the ECG channel, which is one reason the neonatal guideline asks for that channel.

**Pulse.** An electrode over a scalp artery rocks with each pulse, producing **slow, rhythmic waves at one electrode**, following each QRS with a short delay. Moving the electrode removes it.

**Sweat.** A warm child sweats, and the changing skin potential produces **very slow, high-amplitude drift**, usually frontal or temporal. It is slower than any cerebral rhythm and it follows the temperature of the room.

**Glossokinetic.** The tongue is a dipole too, and its movement with talking, crying or feeding produces **slow frontal and temporal waves**. It occurs with the activity that generates it and stops when the child is quiet.
keyPoints: Eye blink: symmetric downward deflection at Fp1 and Fp2 in bipolar montages, frontal only, because the positive cornea rotates upward.
Lateral eye movement: opposite polarity at F7 and F8, with brief lateral rectus spikes at the start of each saccade.
ECG artifact is time-locked to the QRS and often prominent in infants; pulse artifact is slow and rhythmic at one electrode, following each QRS with a short delay.
Muscle disappears in sleep; sweat is very slow, high-amplitude drift in a warm child; glossokinetic waves come with tongue movement.

question.question: A 3-year-old's record shows brief, sharp transients at F7 and F8 with opposite polarity, each followed by a slow wave of the same opposite polarity, recurring irregularly while the child looks around the room. What is the most likely explanation, and how do you confirm it?
options: Lateral eye movements with lateral rectus spikes: the mirror-image polarity across F7 and F8 is the signature, and the video shows the eyes moving
Bilateral independent frontotemporal sharp waves: report them as epileptiform
Electrode pops at F7 and F8: check impedance
Glossokinetic artifact: check whether the child is talking
question.explanation: A horizontal saccade carries the positive cornea toward one side, so F7 and F8 deflect in opposite directions, and the brief lateral rectus spike at the start of the movement precedes the slower eye-movement wave. The mirror image across the hemispheres and the timing with looking around are the proof, and the video confirms it. Bilateral independent sharp waves would not be locked in mirror-image polarity to each other. Electrode pops are abrupt, steep and confined to one electrode without a paired opposite deflection. Glossokinetic artifact is slow and comes with tongue movement, and it lacks the sharp lateral rectus spike.

sections.title: Non-physiologic artifacts: electrodes, lines and equipment
sections.content:
The second group of artifacts comes from the recording system and the room, and each has a mechanical signature.

**Electrode pop.** A poor contact or a sudden change in the electrode-gel-skin interface produces an **abrupt, very steep deflection confined to one electrode**. It is the sharpest thing on the page, which is why it gets called a spike, and it is the easiest artifact to prove: there is **no field in the neighbouring electrodes**. A cerebral spike at T4 would produce smaller deflections at F8, C4 and T6; a pop at T4 produces nothing there at all. Because the electrode is input to two channels in a bipolar chain, a pop can even produce a false phase reversal, so the absence of a field, not the presence of a reversal, is the test.

**60 Hz line noise.** Mains interference produces a **thick, monotonous band** in one or more channels. When it affects one channel, that electrode's impedance is high and the fix is at the scalp. When it affects all channels, the reference or ground is the problem. The notch filter hides it but does not fix it, as [[m01-signals|Module 1]] noted, and a channel full of line noise may be hiding a real finding underneath.

**High-frequency oscillatory ventilation.** In the NICU, an oscillating ventilator shakes the whole baby at its set rate and produces **rhythmic activity at the ventilator rate across many channels**. It is monotonous, it does not evolve, and it matches the ventilator setting exactly. The next section returns to it as the most important rhythmic imitator of a neonatal seizure.

**The general principle**

Equipment artifact is regular in a way that brains are not. Line noise has a fixed frequency; a ventilator has a set rate; a pop has no field. When a waveform is too regular, too confined, or too exactly matched to a machine, look at the machine. Most of these artifacts are also visible to the technologist at the time of recording, so the technologist's notes are part of the read: an impedance problem noted at T4 explains a T4 pop without further work.
keyPoints: Electrode pop: an abrupt, very steep deflection confined to one electrode, with no field in its neighbours.
60 Hz line noise is a thick monotonous band; in one channel it means high impedance at that electrode, and the fix is at the scalp.
High-frequency oscillatory ventilation produces rhythmic activity at the ventilator rate across many channels that does not evolve.
Equipment artifact is regular, confined or machine-matched in ways cerebral activity is not; the technologist's notes are part of the read.

question.question: A spike appears at T4 alone, with no deflection at F8, C4 or T6 in any montage, recurring several times through the record. What is it most likely to be, and what settles it?
options: A right mid-temporal spike; the recurrence confirms it is cerebral
ECG artifact; line it up with the ECG channel
A deep right temporal generator; add a sphenoidal electrode
An electrode pop; the absence of any physiologic field at the neighbouring electrodes settles it
question.explanation: A cerebral spike at T4 would produce smaller deflections at F8, C4 and T6, because a scalp field falls off with distance rather than stopping at one electrode. A transient with no field at all is an electrode artifact, and its abrupt, steep shape is typical of a pop. Recurrence does not make it cerebral, because pops recur as long as the contact is poor. ECG artifact is time-locked to the QRS and usually visible in more than one channel, and lining it up with the ECG channel would show no relationship here. A deep generator explains a discharge that is small or absent at the scalp, not one that is large at a single electrode with nothing around it.

sections.title: Rhythmic artifacts of infancy and the ICU
sections.content:
The artifacts that cause the most harm in pediatric practice are rhythmic, because rhythmic activity is what a seizure looks like, and a rhythmic artifact in a neonate or a ventilated child can lead to an antiseizure drug the child did not need.

**Sucking, patting and rocking.** An infant who is fed, patted or rocked moves rhythmically, and so do the electrodes. The result is **rhythmic activity at the rate of the movement**, which can be in the delta or theta range and can look like a rhythmic discharge. The proof is the **video**: the pattern begins with the movement and **stops when the movement stops**. A nurse's hand on the baby's back is a common generator of "rhythmic delta" in the NICU.

**High-frequency oscillatory ventilation.** The oscillator shakes the infant at its set frequency, producing rhythmic activity across many channels at that rate. It runs for as long as the ventilator does, unchanged, and it matches the setting exactly.

**Evolution is the discriminator**

Rhythmic artifact **does not evolve**. A seizure changes over its course in **frequency, morphology or location**, as [[m10-seizures-status|Module 10]] defines, and the neonatal seizure definition in [[m07-neonatal-abnormal|Module 7]] rests on the same idea. Patting stays at the rate of patting; a ventilator stays at the rate of the ventilator; a seizure speeds up, slows down, changes shape and spreads. Ten minutes of perfectly regular rhythmic activity in every channel is a machine, not a brain.

Because the stakes are a drug, the rule is absolute: **always check the video before calling a neonatal or ICU seizure**. If there is no video, say so in the report and describe the pattern as rhythmic activity of uncertain origin rather than as a seizure. And look for the generator: the ventilator's set rate, the nurse's hand, the feeding. When the generator is found, the report can say what the rhythmic activity was, which is more useful to the team than an equivocal description.
keyPoints: Sucking, patting and rocking produce rhythmic activity at the rate of the movement; the video shows it stopping when the movement stops.
High-frequency oscillatory ventilation produces rhythmic activity at the ventilator rate across many channels.
Rhythmic artifact does not evolve in frequency, morphology or location the way a seizure does.
Always check the video before calling a neonatal or ICU seizure.

question.question: A 3-week-old on high-frequency oscillatory ventilation shows 10 Hz rhythmic activity in every channel for 20 minutes, unchanged in frequency. Seizure or artifact, and what do you check?
options: Seizure: 20 minutes of rhythmic activity exceeds the 10-second neonatal seizure threshold, so treat
Artifact: it is diffuse, it matches a ventilator rate, and it does not evolve; check the ventilator setting
Seizure: 10 Hz is too fast for a ventilator, so the activity must be cerebral
Uncertain: order a repeat study off the ventilator before deciding
question.explanation: Rhythmic activity in every channel, at one unchanging frequency, for 20 minutes is the signature of a machine. A seizure evolves in frequency, morphology or location and has a field that makes anatomical sense, not a uniform presence in every channel. The neonatal seizure definition does require at least 10 seconds, but it also requires an evolving pattern, and duration alone never makes a seizure. A ventilator rate that matches the observed frequency is the confirmation, and checking the setting takes seconds. Taking the infant off the ventilator to repeat the study is neither safe nor necessary when the setting and the video answer the question.

sections.title: A method for deciding: cerebral or not
sections.content:
Put the rules together into a routine you can apply to any doubtful waveform.

1. **Field.** Does it have a plausible scalp distribution, with a maximum and a gradient to its neighbours? If not, it is not cerebral.
2. **Physiology.** Does it match a known generator: the QRS on the ECG channel, the eyes or tongue on video, an artery under an electrode, a warm room?
3. **Regularity.** Is it too regular, too monotonous or too exactly matched to a machine to be biological?
4. **State and behaviour.** Does it appear only with chewing, crying, feeding or patting, and stop when the behaviour stops? Does muscle vanish in sleep?
5. **Video.** Look. For any rhythmic pattern in a neonate or an ICU patient, the video is mandatory.
6. **Technologist's notes.** Impedance problems, movement and interventions are recorded at the time and explain much of what you see.

The table collects the artifacts in this module with their appearance and their proof.

| Artifact | What it looks like | How to confirm |
|---|---|---|
| Eye blink | Symmetric downward deflection at Fp1 and Fp2 in bipolar montages; the cornea is positive and rotates up | Frontal only, no posterior field; eyes on video |
| Lateral eye movement | Opposite polarity at F7 and F8; brief lateral rectus spikes at the start of each saccade | Mirror image across hemispheres |
| Electrode pop | Abrupt, very steep deflection confined to one electrode | No field in neighbouring electrodes |
| Muscle | Very fast, spiky activity, often temporal, during chewing or crying | Disappears in sleep or with relaxation |
| ECG | Sharp transient time-locked to the QRS, often prominent in infants | Line up with the ECG channel |
| Pulse | Slow, rhythmic waves at one electrode, following each QRS with a short delay | Electrode over an artery; moving it removes the artifact |
| Sweat | Very slow, high-amplitude drift | Frontal or temporal, in a warm child |
| 60 Hz line noise | Thick monotonous band in one or more channels | Check impedance of those electrodes |
| Sucking, patting, rocking | Rhythmic activity at the rate of the movement | Video; stops when the movement stops |
| High-frequency oscillatory ventilation | Rhythmic activity at the ventilator rate across many channels | Does not evolve; matches the ventilator setting |
| Glossokinetic | Slow frontal and temporal waves with tongue movement | Occurs with talking, crying or feeding |

The sign-off for this module is ten artifacts correctly labelled on real records, at least three of them from infants or the ICU. Label each one with its proof, not just its name: "ECG artifact, time-locked to the QRS" is a labelled artifact; "artifact" is a guess.
keyPoints: Test field, physiology, regularity, state and behaviour, then the video and the technologist's notes.
Each artifact has a proof: the ECG channel, the video, the impedance, the ventilator setting, the moved electrode.
Label an artifact with its proof, not just its name.
For any rhythmic pattern in a neonate or ICU patient, the video is mandatory.

question.question: A 4-month-old has rhythmic 2 Hz frontal waves that appear during feeding. What do you check, and what result would confirm artifact?
options: The ECG channel; artifact is confirmed if the waves are time-locked to the QRS
The impedance at Fp1 and Fp2; artifact is confirmed if it is high
The video for sucking, and whether the pattern stops when feeding stops
The high-frequency filter; artifact is confirmed if the waves disappear when it is lowered
question.explanation: Rhythmic frontal waves that appear with feeding point to sucking or glossokinetic artifact, and the proof is behavioural: the video shows the sucking, and the pattern stops when the feeding stops. A 2 Hz rhythm at the rate of sucking is not time-locked to the QRS, so the ECG channel would not explain it. High impedance produces line noise or pops, not a rhythmic delta that follows feeding. Lowering the high-frequency filter attenuates fast activity and would not remove a 2 Hz wave; making a finding disappear with a filter is never the way to prove artifact.

quiz.question: A 2-month-old's record shows a sharp transient in several right-sided channels, recurring about twice a second with a fixed interval. What is the first step in evaluating it?
options: Line it up with the ECG channel, because a sharp transient recurring at a fixed interval near the heart rate is ECG artifact until proven otherwise
Report right hemispheric periodic discharges
Lower the high-frequency filter to see whether it persists
Add a transverse montage to find the phase reversal
quiz.explanation: A sharp transient recurring at a fixed interval in the range of an infant's heart rate is ECG artifact until proven otherwise, and the proof is the ECG channel, which is one reason the neonatal guideline asks for it. Reporting periodic discharges without excluding the heart is the over-read the module warns against. Lowering the high-frequency filter changes morphology and proves nothing about origin. A transverse montage might show an apparent maximum, but a phase reversal does not distinguish a cerebral source from a large extracerebral one; only finding the generator does.

quiz.question: A record from a warm, crying 18-month-old shows very slow, high-amplitude drift over the frontal and temporal regions, along with very fast spiky activity over both temporal regions. Which pairing of explanations is most likely?
options: Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta and bilateral temporal spikes
Sweat artifact and muscle artifact, both of which will settle when the child is cooled and calm or asleep
Electrode pops and line noise
Glossokinetic artifact and lateral rectus spikes
quiz.explanation: Very slow, high-amplitude drift in a warm child over the frontal or temporal regions is sweat, and very fast, spiky temporal activity in a crying child is temporalis muscle. Both are proved by their behaviour: sweat follows the temperature, and muscle disappears with relaxation or sleep. Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta is rhythmic, not a slow drift, and temporal spikes would have a field and a morphology rather than continuous fast activity. Electrode pops are abrupt and confined to one electrode, and line noise is a monotonous band, neither of which fits. Glossokinetic waves are slow but come specifically with tongue movement, and lateral rectus spikes are brief mirror-image transients at F7 and F8 rather than continuous temporal muscle.

quiz.question: A PICU nurse pages about rhythmic 3 Hz activity that has appeared in the frontal channels of a sedated 5-year-old's continuous EEG. The pattern started 4 minutes ago and has not changed. Before calling it a seizure, which step is mandatory?
options: Give a benzodiazepine and watch for the pattern to stop
Raise the low-frequency filter to remove it if it is artifact
Look at the video for a generator such as patting, chest physiotherapy or a device, and check whether the pattern evolves
Wait until it reaches 10 minutes, which defines status epilepticus
quiz.explanation: Rhythmic activity that begins abruptly and stays at one frequency for minutes without evolving is the profile of a mechanical generator, and in the PICU that is often a hand, a physiotherapy device or a pump. The video is the mandatory check before calling a neonatal or ICU seizure, and evolution in frequency, morphology or location is what distinguishes a seizure from a rhythm. Giving a benzodiazepine to test the hypothesis exposes a child to a drug when the video would have answered the question. Filters cannot prove artifact. Waiting for a duration threshold does not help, because artifact will happily run for 10 minutes too.

quiz.question: A neonatal record shows slow, rhythmic waves at one electrode, C3, each one following a QRS complex on the ECG channel after a short delay. Nothing similar appears at F3, P3 or T3. What is it, and what removes it?
options: Pulse artifact from an electrode over a scalp artery; moving the electrode removes it
A left central periodic discharge; it will require treatment
ECG artifact; the notch filter removes it
Sucking artifact; it stops when the feed stops
quiz.explanation: Slow, rhythmic waves at a single electrode that follow each QRS with a short delay are pulse artifact: the electrode is rocking on an artery with each heartbeat. The absence of any field at the neighbouring electrodes confirms that it is not cerebral, and moving the electrode off the artery removes it. A periodic discharge would have a field and would not be tied to the pulse. ECG artifact is a sharp transient synchronous with the QRS, not a delayed slow wave, and the notch filter removes line frequency, not either kind of cardiac artifact. Sucking artifact follows feeding, not the heartbeat.

quiz.question: A resident labels an artifact on a real record simply as "artifact" during the sign-off exercise. The faculty reader asks for more. What does a complete label contain?
options: The channel in which the artifact was largest
The artifact's name together with the evidence that proves it, such as "ECG artifact, time-locked to the QRS" or "electrode pop, no field at neighbouring electrodes"
The filter setting that made the artifact disappear
The page number and time of the artifact
quiz.explanation: The skill being tested is not spotting something odd but proving what it is, so the label names the artifact and the observation that proves it: the generator on the ECG channel or the video, the absence of a field, the ventilator setting, the response to moving an electrode. Naming the channel or the time locates the waveform without identifying it. A filter setting that makes something disappear proves nothing about origin, because filters remove cerebral activity just as readily as artifact.
